notes:
## Transformer (deep learning)
In deep learning, the transformer is a family of artificial neural network architectures based on the multi-head attention mechanism, in which input data such as text, images, or audio is  converted to a sequence of numerical representations called tokens, and each token is converted into a vector through an embedding layer. At each layer, each token is then contextualized within the scope of the context window with other (unmasked) tokens via a parallel multi-head attention mechanism, allowing the signal for key tokens to be amplified and less important tokens to be diminished. Because self-attention alone is permutation-invariant, transformers inject positional information, typically through positional encodings or learned positional embeddings, so token order can affect the output.
Because transformers do not process tokens one at a time, their computations can be parallelized across sequence positions during training more readily than those of recurrent neural networks like long short-term memory (LSTM). Later variations have been widely adopted for training large language models (LLMs) on large (language) datasets.

## Mamba (deep learning architecture)
Mamba is a deep learning architecture focused on sequence modeling. It was developed by two researchers Albert Gu from Carnegie Mellon University and Tri Dao from Princeton University to address some limitations of transformer models, especially in processing long sequences, and it is based on the Structured State Space sequence (S4) model.

## Self-supervised learning
Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a paradigm in machine learning where a model is trained on a task using the data itself to generate supervisory signals, rather than relying on externally-provided labels. In the context of neural networks, self-supervised learning aims to leverage inherent structures or relationships within the input data to create meaningful training signals. SSL tasks are designed so that solving them requires capturing essential features or relationships in the data. The input data is typically augmented or transformed in a way that creates pairs of related samples, where one sample serves as the input, and the other is used to formulate the supervisory signal. This augmentation can involve introducing noise, cropping, rotation, or other transformations. Self-supervised learning more closely imitates the way humans learn to classify objects.
During SSL, the model learns in two steps. First, the task is solved based on an auxiliary or pretext classification task using pseudo-labels, which help to initialize the model parameters. Next, the actual task is performed with supervised or unsupervised learning.

## List of large language models
A large language model (LLM) is a type of machine learning model designed for natural language processing tasks such as language generation. LLMs are language models with many parameters, and are trained with self-supervised learning on a vast amount of text.

plan.title: How ChatGPT-Style Language Models Actually Work
plan.description: Large language models like ChatGPT predict text using a transformer and attention. This video explains tokens, vectors, attention and self-supervised training in plain language.

beats.narration: How can a machine write an essay, explain a joke, or fix your code? It has no mind like yours. Underneath, it does one surprisingly simple thing, over and over.

props.title: How do ChatGPT-style models work?
props.subtitle: One simple trick, repeated at huge scale

beats.narration: Think of your phone's autocomplete. You type a few words, and it guesses the next one. A large language model is that idea, grown enormously and made far smarter.

props.alt: person typing a message on a phone

beats.narration: A large language model, or LLM, is a machine learning model with many parameters, trained on a vast amount of text. Its job is language generation.

props.definition: A machine learning model with many parameters, trained on a vast amount of text, designed for tasks such as language generation.

beats.narration: But computers do not read words. So first, text is chopped into pieces called tokens. Each token then becomes a list of numbers, a vector, through an embedding layer.
Tokens become vectors. Then position is added, because order matters. Order changes the output: dog bites man means something very different from man bites dog.
Now comes the key idea of the transformer: attention. Each token looks at the other tokens around it, and decides which ones matter most for its own meaning.
Attention weighs them. Key tokens are amplified, and less important ones are diminished. The result is context-rich vectors, where each word carries the meaning of its neighbors.

This happens in many heads at once, which is why it is called multi-head attention. And because tokens are not handled one at a time, training can run in parallel. That is why transformers scale so well.

props.text: Many attention heads work in parallel, so transformers scale.

beats.narration: So how does it learn? Nobody labels billions of sentences by hand. Instead, the text itself provides the answer. Hide the next word, and ask the model to guess it.

props.alt: rows of books in a large library

beats.narration: This is self-supervised learning: the data generates its own training signal, instead of relying on outside labels. Guess, check against the real text, adjust, and repeat across a vast amount of writing.
Repeat that enormous number of times, and the model has to capture the patterns and relationships in language to keep guessing well. Grammar, facts and style all emerge from that single goal.

props.text: SSL tasks are designed so that solving them requires capturing essential features or relationships in the data.

beats.narration: Transformers also have rivals. Mamba, built by Albert Gu and Tri Dao, targets limits of transformers on long sequences. The field is still evolving.
So the whole idea fits in two lines. The transformer is attention over tokens. LLMs are trained on vast text. Together, they predict one token at a time, and that prediction becomes fluent writing.
